title: Clinical teaming: AI accuracy may worsen joint decisions
desc: Emphasizes self-calibration, selective assignment and local testing rather than assuming seniority or human involvement ensures benefit.

kps.k: AI’s standalone accuracy does not establish that human–AI teams perform better.
kps.d: The cluster challenges automatic assumptions of either augmentation or replacement. In Agarwal and colleagues’ 227-radiologist experiment, CheXpert achieved an AUC of 0.85 and outperformed 78% of participants, yet assistance produced no significant average diagnostic improvement and increased assessment time by about 4%. Clinical history improved accuracy, showing that humans held useful additional information. A fitted combination benchmark reached an AUC of 0.88, but this represents unrealized potential, not observed team performance. Results differ across settings: The ABC's of Who Benefits from Working with AI reports average accuracy gains, while The algorithm will see you now cites favorable mammography trials.

qs.q: First, we see that AI with an AUC of 0.85 is more accurate than 78% of humans, which means that a majority of radiologists would do better by simply following the AI prediction.
qs.a: Combining Human Expertise with Artificial Intelligence: Experimental Evidence from Radiology · Academia · 2023

qs.q: We find that AI assistance improves prediction accuracy on average and with heteroge- neous impacts across individuals.
qs.a: The ABC's of Who Benefits from Working with AI: Ability, Beliefs, and Calibration · Academia · 2024

kps.k: Who benefits depends on more than seniority or baseline skill; self-knowledge and case-level confidence may matter.
kps.d: The radiologist heterogeneity analysis examines 140 radiologists, 324 cases and 15 pathologies, finding that experience, subspecialty, AI familiarity and baseline performance do not reliably predict gains. It uses shrinkage and split sampling to limit sampling noise and spurious baseline–gain correlations. This challenges reported experience-based associations without proving that experience never matters. The ABC's study instead identifies self-calibration: holding ability fixed, a one-standard-deviation increase corresponds to a 20% larger assistance effect, with low-ability, well-calibrated participants benefiting most. These findings concern different predictors and settings, not a direct contradiction. Self-calibration about ability also differs from diagnostic probability calibration. Agarwal and colleagues identify case-level confidence patterns and explicitly describe Yu et al.’s heterogeneity findings as a secondary analysis of their data, not independent replication.

qs.q: We found that experience-based radiologist characteristics, including years of experience, subspecialty in thoracic radiology and experience with AI tools, did not serve as reliable predictors of treatment effect, in terms of both calibration performance and discrimination performance.
qs.a: Heterogeneity and predictors of the effects of AI assistance on radiologists · Academia · 2024

qs.q: Holding baseline ability fixed, a one standard deviation increase in calibration increases the average treatment e↵ect of AI assistance by 20 percent.
qs.a: The ABC's of Who Benefits from Working with AI: Ability, Beliefs, and Calibration · Academia · 2024

kps.k: Human involvement can transmit AI errors, but the proposed mechanisms differ and remain qualified.
kps.d: The heterogeneity study associates larger AI errors with worse assisted performance; the relationship is clearer for absolute probability error than for AUROC. Its authors explicitly decline to infer a cognitive mechanism because case characteristics and interpretation remain intertwined. Agarwal and colleagues offer a fitted model combining underweighting of AI with neglect of dependence between human and AI signals; underweighting alone cannot explain deterioration from uncertain AI advice. By contrast, The algorithm will see you now emphasizes reliance on incorrect guidance or absent prompts, citing a 2011 review in which incorrect guidance made clinicians 26% more likely to err than unaided peers. These accounts caution against treating all collaboration failures as simple overtrust or assuming that a human reviewer necessarily corrects model mistakes.

qs.q: In addition to investigating the radiologist characteristics that can impact AI’s treatment effect, we showed that higher-quality AI assistance leads to better treatment effects in terms of calibration performance measured by absolute error, whereas the trend was unclear in terms of discrimination performance measured by AUROC.
qs.a: Heterogeneity and predictors of the effects of AI assistance on radiologists · Academia · 2024

qs.q: We also identify systematic errors in belief updating; specifically radiologists exhibit automation neglect (e.g., radiologists underweight the AI prediction relative to their own) and incorrectly treat the AI prediction and their own signals as conditionally independent.
qs.a: Combining Human Expertise with Artificial Intelligence: Experimental Evidence from Radiology · Academia · 2023

kps.k: Selective task assignment may outperform routine assistance, but autonomy is a conditional design choice rather than an established remedy.
kps.d: Agarwal and colleagues’ economic model trades diagnostic quality against radiologist time and assumes zero marginal cost for AI predictions. Under observed behavior, it assigns most cases to either humans alone or AI alone. Under correct information combination, assistance becomes optimal for more cases, particularly when AI is uncertain. This is a modeled policy, not a tested deployment outcome; it abstracts from pathology interactions, strategic responses, organizational incentives and regulation. The algorithm will see you now tentatively suggests that autonomy could avoid some interaction failures, but stresses technical, insurance and regulatory barriers, including the need to reject unsuitable or out-of-scope images.

qs.q: We assume that the AI signal can always be obtained at zero marginal cost and implement a classifier that decides, as a function of the AI prediction, to delegate a patient to either be diagnosed by a human, a human with access to the AI, or the AI alone.
qs.a: Combining Human Expertise with Artificial Intelligence: Experimental Evidence from Radiology · Academia · 2023

qs.q: Autonomous tools have to clear a much higher bar: they must demonstrate that the AI tool will refuse to read any scan that is blurry, uses an unusual scanner, or is outside its competence.
qs.a: The algorithm will see you now · Market & press · 2025

kps.k: Deployment needs local and individual testing because benchmark results may not transfer to clinical workflows.
kps.d: The algorithm will see you now attributes transfer failures to selective datasets, overfitting, equipment differences and demographic underrepresentation, citing poorer cross-hospital pneumonia detection and difficulties with subtle disease. It recommends local retraining or revalidation. The heterogeneity study adds testing of each clinician’s response on representative patient cases rather than allocating assistance by seniority alone. The radiology experiments use retrospective cases and diagnostic standards rather than patient health outcomes; Agarwal and colleagues’ NBER working paper uses aggregated specialist judgments, not definitive ground truth. Training, richer explanations and improved self-calibration remain research directions: the ABC's estimate that eliminating miscalibration could nearly double inequality reduction is counterfactual, not evidence that an intervention achieves it.

qs.q: This means that individual hospitals or departments would need to retrain or revalidate today’s crop of tools before adopting them, even if they have been proven elsewhere.
qs.a: The algorithm will see you now · Market & press · 2025

qs.q: Without reliable predictors, it is necessary to measure radiologists’ response to AI assistance under realistic simulations of deployment settings before deciding whether to provide AI assistance to different radiologists.
qs.a: Heterogeneity and predictors of the effects of AI assistance on radiologists · Academia · 2024

kps.k: Task-level substitution and time savings do not directly imply occupation-wide job losses.
kps.d: Langlotz’s 2025, non-peer-reviewed workforce preprint predicts that rising imaging demand will offset productivity gains over five years, slowing growth in radiologist demand rather than reducing employment. Its task model expects study delegation and report drafting to save more time than detection and triage. A sensitivity scenario projects a 35% reduction in hours, not jobs. The employment conclusion depends on continued imaging growth, which the model does not explicitly estimate; many task assumptions rely on author judgment. Phased adoption, investment constraints and resistance to AI-only interpretation make effects upper-end projections, while omitted monitoring and oversight work may alter net savings. This complements, rather than contradicts, the experimental distinction between substitution on particular diagnoses and complementarity across the occupation’s wider task bundle.

qs.q: The productivity gains from AI are likely to be offset by continued growth in imaging volumes, causing continued growth in the need for radiologists, albeit at a slower rate.
qs.a: The Effect of AI on the Radiologist Workforce: A Task-Based Analysis · Academia · 2025

qs.q: Although we find that human radiologists and AI are substitutes on specific tasks (as defined by diagnosis of particular cases), they may still be complements in the overall production function which involves a bundle of different tasks (Acemoglu and Autor, 2011).
qs.a: Combining Human Expertise with Artificial Intelligence: Experimental Evidence from Radiology · Academia · 2023

kps.k: Radiology offers evidence about collaboration design, not a universal forecast for generative AI or other professions.
kps.d: The substantive implication is to evaluate the deployed human–AI system, its task allocation and its net workload rather than infer outcomes from model accuracy alone. However, the principal radiology experiments study image-classification assistance, and their short-run designs leave learning and interface improvements unresolved. Agarwal and colleagues explicitly warn that their preference for separate human and AI work may not hold for generative AI. Langlotz’s workforce projections also depend on U.S.-centric task and demand assumptions. Applying these findings to legal work or other knowledge occupations therefore requires fresh evidence about their workflows, human checking costs and demand responses.

qs.q: For instance, our observation that humans optimally work next to as opposed to with AI may not necessarily hold for other cases such as generative AI.
qs.a: Combining Human Expertise with Artificial Intelligence: Experimental Evidence from Radiology · Academia · 2023

qs.q: We were unable to assess whether radiologists improved in incorporating AI predictions over time as they encountered more patient cases.
qs.a: Heterogeneity and predictors of the effects of AI assistance on radiologists · Academia · 2024

vlens.an: The curated academia-and-research sources collectively accept the proposition’s core warning that standalone AI accuracy and the presence of a human reviewer do not guarantee improved joint decisions. They materially develop it through experimental evidence of no significant average benefit despite strong AI performance, confidence-dependent harms, systematic information-combination errors, substantial clinician-level heterogeneity, and the weak predictive value of seniority, subspecialty, AI familiarity, or baseline skill. They also add concrete deployment implications: assess self-calibration, use selective rather than routine assignment where warranted, and test individual clinicians with the specific AI system on locally representative cases. Material internal variation remains. One study reports average gains from assistance and identifies self-calibration as a key moderator, whereas the principal radiology experiment finds no significant average improvement; these results arise in different tasks and populations rather than forming a direct contradiction. The proposed mechanisms also differ: one analysis models belief-updating errors, while another associates inaccurate AI with worse assisted performance but declines to identify a cognitive mechanism. The workforce preprint redirects from decision quality to task productivity and demand, projecting time savings without near-term job loss under uncertain imaging-growth assumptions. Across the sources, selective assignment, training benefits, and workforce outcomes remain conditional or modelled rather than established deployment results, and the radiology findings are not presented as automatically transferable to generative AI or other professions.

qs.q: In contrast, AI assistance does not significantly improve average performance.
qs.a: Combining Human Expertise with Artificial Intelligence: Experimental Evidence from Radiology · Academia · 2023

qs.q: Without reliable predictors, it is necessary to measure radiologists’ response to AI assistance under realistic simulations of deployment settings before deciding whether to provide AI assistance to different radiologists.
qs.a: Heterogeneity and predictors of the effects of AI assistance on radiologists · Academia · 2024

vlens.an: The selected press source, “The algorithm will see you now,” accepts the proposition that benchmark accuracy and the mere presence of a clinician do not ensure better joint decisions. It materially extends that proposition by explaining why performance may deteriorate in deployment: hospital-specific data and equipment limit transferability; selectively constructed datasets underrepresent ambiguous cases and some demographic groups; and clinicians may propagate errors from incorrect guidance or interpret missing prompts as reassurance. It therefore argues for local retraining or revalidation rather than relying on benchmark results. Its position is not uniformly anti-assistance: it acknowledges favorable human–AI mammography trials and tentatively considers autonomy as a way to avoid some interaction failures. However, autonomy is presented as conditional rather than proven, given technical limitations and the higher regulatory and safety bar for systems operating without physician review. This characterizes the supplied source only, not market analysts, consultancies or the press generally.

qs.q: This means that individual hospitals or departments would need to retrain or revalidate today’s crop of tools before adopting them, even if they have been proven elsewhere.
qs.a: The algorithm will see you now · Market & press · 2025

qs.q: Another [review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3240751/), this time from 2011, found that when a system gave incorrect guidance, clinicians were 26 percent more likely to make a wrong decision than unaided peers.
qs.a: The algorithm will see you now · Market & press · 2025

elens.an: The curated 2023–2024 sources collectively accept the proposition that standalone AI accuracy and the mere presence of a human do not guarantee better joint decisions, and materially develop it with evidence about why benefits vary and how deployment might respond. Their common reasoning is that team performance depends on the interaction among model reliability, the user’s interpretation of AI signals, self-knowledge and case-level conditions—not simply seniority, baseline skill or aggregate model performance. Material variation remains. The ABC study finds positive average assistance effects in a non-clinical prediction task and identifies self-calibration, especially among lower-ability participants, as a key moderator. The radiology experiment—originally from 2023 but subsequently revised—finds no significant average improvement despite strong AI performance, models systematic belief-updating errors and conditionally favors selective human-only, AI-only or assisted assignment. The related radiologist analysis finds substantial individual heterogeneity, rejects experience-based characteristics as reliable allocation rules and recommends realistic individual testing. These findings therefore strengthen the cluster’s design-oriented caution, while not establishing that selective assignment, training or calibration interventions will generalize to generative AI or other workflows.

qs.q: In contrast, AI assistance does not significantly improve average performance.
qs.a: Combining Human Expertise with Artificial Intelligence: Experimental Evidence from Radiology · Academia · 2023

qs.q: Holding baseline ability fixed, a one standard deviation increase in calibration increases the average treatment e↵ect of AI assistance by 20 percent.
qs.a: The ABC's of Who Benefits from Working with AI: Ability, Beliefs, and Calibration · Academia · 2024

elens.an: The 2025 sources collectively accept or remain compatible with the proposition’s rejection of accuracy-led assumptions and materially extend it toward deployment at scale. “The algorithm will see you now” directly develops the proposition: benchmark results may deteriorate in clinical settings because of dataset selection, cross-hospital differences and clinician responses to erroneous or missing prompts. It therefore supports local retraining or revalidation and treats autonomous deployment as conditional on safeguards rather than as an established cure for human–AI interaction failures. Langlotz’s non-peer-reviewed workforce preprint redirects attention from joint diagnostic quality to task-level productivity, adoption and labour demand. It neither establishes nor contests the proposition’s teaming mechanisms; instead, it adds that even substantial modelled time savings would not automatically yield occupation-wide displacement, especially where implementation is phased, incomplete and resisted. Material variation thus lies in outcome and evidence type: one source focuses on observed and reported clinical-performance failures and deployment controls, while the other offers conditional five-year workforce projections based partly on author judgment and an unmodelled continuation of imaging-demand growth. Taken together, this curated 2025 evidence builds on the proposition by showing that scaled adoption must be evaluated locally at the level of workflows, human responses, task allocation, implementation constraints and net workload—not inferred from standalone model accuracy or theoretical task savings.

qs.q: This means that individual hospitals or departments would need to retrain or revalidate today’s crop of tools before adopting them, even if they have been proven elsewhere.
qs.a: The algorithm will see you now · Market & press · 2025

qs.q: It is unlikely that all organizations will adopt all these algorithms.
qs.a: The Effect of AI on the Radiologist Workforce: A Task-Based Analysis · Academia · 2025
